summary: Number 29 of South Korean Interim Government Activities, prepared by the National Economic Board for USAMGIK, covers February 1948. Cold-war tension dominates: leftist sabotage and strikes from 7 February, the UN Interim Committee's 27 February decision to observe elections in South Korea alone, the split between Rhee, Kim Koo and Kimm Kiu-sic, and the walkout of Speaker Kimm and 30 legislators that crippled the Interim Legislative Assembly. The report also records completion of rice collection at 97.6 per cent of quota, continued industrial shortages of bituminous coal, power and parts, record revenues exceeding expenditures for the first time since liberation, price indexes still rising, vested property disposal and land reform, police and civil-liberties reforms ahead of the May elections, and a 58 per cent rise in northern refugees. Detailed statistical tables on population, prices, production, trade, finance and labor, plus feature studies on the Korean National Youth, women and the flag, make it a rich source for historians of the occupation.
highlights: UN Interim Committee decided on 27 February to witness elections in South Korea alone, overshadowing all other developments.
Leftists began a revolt on 7 February; sabotage and riots occurred but no nation-wide general strike developed.
Speaker Kimm Kiu-sic and 30 legislators resigned from KILA over an 'Urgent Proposal' to the UN, halting the Assembly.
Rice collection ended 15 February with 97.6 per cent of the quota collected.
February revenues exceeded expenditures for the first time since liberation; note circulation fell 722 million won.
Refugee inflow from north of the 38th parallel rose 58 per cent over January; 4,074 processed in February.
Seoul retail price index reached 2,310, over 23 times the August 1945 level, rising for the ninth straight month.
Police administrative authority was transferred from national to provincial control as a safeguard against a police state.

sections.title: Front matter
sections.summary: Cover of No. 29 (February 1948), prepared by the National Economic Board for USAMGIK (call number M 105.13:29), followed by Google scan pages and the printed contents (pp. i-v). The contents list Parts I-VI: basic aspects, production and supply, public services, finance, government and politics, and social affairs, with paragraph-level page references.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Reviews February 1948 under cold-war tension: the leftist revolt and sabotage from 7 February, the UN Interim Committee's 27 February decision to observe South-only elections, and the walkout of Speaker Kimm Kiu-sic with 30 legislators from KILA. Also notes a 58 per cent refugee increase, civil-rights measures, vested property leasing, industrial shortages, first revenue surplus and women's activities.

sections.title: Part I: Basic Aspects
sections.summary: Population and foreign affairs, and vested property.

sections.title: Section 1: Population and Foreign Affairs
sections.summary: Refugees from the North rose 58 per cent over January (4,074 processed in February), and cumulative movement tables are given. The 1947 Seoul census counts 779,890 adults by occupation, schooling and marital status. Also covers Koreans in Manchuria (about 800,000), plans to close low-standard Osaka Korean schools, SKIG liaison problems in Tokyo, 192 illegal entrants, and draft immigration regulations.

sections.title: Section 2: Vested Property
sections.summary: Vested property sales were held back by scarce reputable Korean buyers and nationalization and land-reform uncertainty, so leasing (299 plants leased), liquidation and corporate reorganization (409 companies examined) were tried; February sales totaled 35 for 4,600,800 won. Also covers 423 audits, the Buddhist property report, textile loans over 200 million won, and 33 million won in new loan applications.

sections.title: Part II: Production and Supply
sections.summary: Food, agriculture, prices, industry, mining, allocation, trade and labor.

sections.title: Section 1: Food Supply
sections.summary: The 1947/48 rice collection ended 15 February at 97.6 per cent of quota (754,579 metric tons), with Cholla-pukto the only province well short. Covers stocks, rationing releases of 96,634 tons, grain imports of only 4,102 tons, ration cuts in Seoul, and projections showing need for 225,000 tons of imported cereals in 1948/49.

sections.title: Section 2: Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries
sections.summary: Covers FAO 1950 census planning, training of 123 crop-reporting employees, and the New Korea Company's status and land evaluation plan for its 324,604 chungbo, to be sold at three times annual crop value over 15 years. Also livestock, straw bags, hemp, sericulture, fuelwood, fisheries training for 350 students, laver exports, the Korean Agricultural Association, and Kyonggi-do 4-H clubs growing to 1,072.

sections.title: Section 3: Prices
sections.summary: Seoul retail prices rose for the ninth straight month: the February index of 2,310 was nearly four per cent above January, while the wholesale index fell to 6,910, more than six per cent below January's record. Grain and food rose, textiles and fuel fell. Tables give prices, controlled prices (rice steady since November 1945) and civilian-supply prices.

sections.title: Section 4: Industrial Production
sections.summary: Industrial output stayed low, with data mostly for January 1948. Flour, noodles, cotton yarn and cloth, paper, nails, briquettes, cement, rubber items and tobacco are reported, with shortages of wheat, pulp, pitch, coal and power; Puksan paper mill resumed after 10 months. Government salterns were idle, and 1947 annual production tables from the Department of Commerce are given.

sections.title: Section 5: Mining and Minerals
sections.summary: January anthracite output reached 41,357 metric tons, 32 per cent above December, though Samchuk and Tanyang missed quotas through power failures, snow and poor transport. Bituminous imports from Japan hit a record 83,330 tons in February, with 50,000 extra tons allotted for power. Pitch for briquettes stayed scarce; gold, silver, tungsten, zinc and lead rose, copper fell.

sections.title: Section 6: Allocations and Distribution
sections.summary: The new Consumer Goods Allocation Board and National Consumer Goods Office confined February to organization; about 22,000,000 won of Civil Service Relief Committee goods were inventoried. Petroleum allocations were reported, and prices were raised effective 1 April. Salt use, ex-Japanese metal stocks and distribution of the 223,000,000 won year-end bonus goods through the FFA and FDA were covered.

sections.title: Section 7: Imports and Exports
sections.summary: Private trade estimates for February were imports of 260 million won against exports of 421 million; January imports were 352 million and exports 348 million, mostly via Hong Kong. New Trustee Shipment and export-loan rules were issued. Government cargoes went to the United States and Japan (laver exports), plus FLC purchases from Hawaii, coal, fertilizer, rice and salt imports.

sections.title: Section 8: Labor
sections.summary: The Seoul Electric Company's union contract with the Tai Han federation was extended pending talks, and a seamen's bargaining election was set for 5-7 March in six ports. Pungkuk Flour Mills agreed to pay back wages. Unions reported 84,363 members; labor-law inspections, pamphlets, radio programs, a labor kiosk and an industrial medical plan followed.

sections.title: Part III: Public Services
sections.summary: Transportation, communications, utilities and public works.

sections.title: Section 1: Transportation
sections.summary: New rail, marine and highway rates took effect in February, rail fares rising 25 per cent (first and second class) and 50 per cent (third). Railroad sabotage from 7 February damaged 52 locomotives and ended night passenger trains. January rail income, freight, passengers and coal use fell; locomotives operative dropped by 26. Marine income rose, a Pusan pier warehouse burned, and a 75-ton crane arrived.

sections.title: Section 2: Communications
sections.summary: Use of communications grew markedly in 1947, with about 7,500 would-be telephone subscribers unserved. January revenue fell from December, though Pusan and Kwangju returns were missing; expenditures rose 1,000,000 won and employees rose for a third month. Postal deposits, insurance, telephone traffic gained; an emergency transmitter was installed, and 20,000 radio receivers were repaired.

sections.title: Section 3: Public Utilities
sections.summary: Power delivered to distributors in February was 72,000,000 KWH, of which 24,000,000 were produced in South Korea, improving on December and January. The Emergency Power Board extended the curfew from 2200 to 2300 and planned year-round control. Chung Pyung and Tang In Ri failures were repaired; sabotage was minor. Seoul tram fares were approved at five won from 5 March.

sections.title: Section 4: Public Works
sections.summary: Mild February weather let road and bridge repairs begin early. Highway man-days reached 171,451. The Bureau of Highways reported 236,753,123.85 won spent on the Seoul-Pusan road, and a Seoul-East Coast road was surveyed. An irrigation and flood program was submitted, 50,000,000 won flood funds allocated, and volunteer fire brigades and the Seoul Firemen's School were started; 149 fires caused 219,143,550 won loss.

sections.title: Part IV: Finance
sections.summary: Government and non-government finance.

sections.title: Section 1: Government Finance
sections.summary: Bank of Chosun notes outstanding fell 722 million won in February, and for the first time revenue deposits exceeded withdrawals, a net 386 million won. Supplementary 1947/48 appropriations of 627 million won were approved. The Military Governor ordered a balanced 1948/49 budget, set at about 22,000 million won of revenue; taxes, guaranteed loans (13,710 million won contingent) and Civilian Supply cash (5,083 million won) are also reported.

sections.title: Section 2: Non-Government Finance
sections.summary: Data cover January only. Cash balances rose over 614 million won and total deposits rose 6,882 million won, over 15 per cent, to 52,208 million. Loans fell 1,062 million won. The section describes the eight financial institutions, gives life and damage insurance figures, and reports the Foreign Exchange Bank's first trade loan, a 352 million won claim on past-due guaranteed loans, and new borrower registration rules.

sections.title: Part V: Government and Politics
sections.summary: Administration, legislature, politics, law, police and interzone affairs.

sections.title: Section 1: Administration
sections.summary: Maj.-Gen. Helmick, Deputy Military Governor, was in Washington 19 January to 4 February to justify GARIOA and rehabilitation funds for 1948/49 and discussed the North Korean power agreement. Civil service ratings, examinations and personnel actions are listed. The National Economic Board approved supplemental budgets, decontrolled silk and raised coal prices. A reorganization plan would cut 40 per cent of bureaus; a vested-land sale ordinance and Military Government personnel figures are included.

sections.title: Section 2: Korean Interim Legislative Assembly
sections.summary: KILA approved the 1947 budget 38 to one on 2 February, and debated the Kukmin College eviction, Koje fishing rights, a nationality law, absentees, rice rationing and a prostitution-bribery rumor. The rightists' Urgent Proposal asking the UN Commission for a South Korean election split the Assembly. It passed amended 40 to 0 on 23 February; Speaker Kimm Kiu-sic and Vice-Speaker Choe Tong-O resigned.

sections.title: Section 3: Political Developments
sections.summary: Politics centered on the UN Commission and whether to hold elections in South Korea alone. Rhee Syngman's rightists favored a separate election, while Kimm Kiu-sic and Kim Koo wanted a North-South leaders' conference and an all-Korea vote. Menon described the parties on 19 February; the three leaders met 10 February. The UN Interim Committee approved a South Korean election 31 to 2 on 27 February.

sections.title: Section 4: Legal Affairs
sections.summary: The Department of Justice published ordinances including an order barring separate Sam Il Day demonstrations, and issued opinions on overtime pay, vested property damage, rice confiscation and transferring vested farm land. Penal items include 191 guards graduated and prison security inspections. Korean courts admitted five northern lawyers, drafted arrest-protection rules and handled a prosecutor-beating complaint; a claims program is being prepared.

sections.title: Section 5: National Police
sections.summary: Police Department recommendations on civil liberties included release after three days without charge, court-appointed jail inspectors, and curbs on graft and brutality. The Military Governor reaffirmed that provincial police chiefs answer to governors, except on organization, administration, finances and personnel. A 7-12 February strike and riot wave brought 1,489 arrests, with 6 police and 29 rioters killed. General Dean commended the arrest of 12 counterfeiters.

sections.title: Section 6: Interzone Activities
sections.summary: More than 45,000 pieces of mail crossed the 38th parallel at Tosong. Radio Pyongyang attacked General Hodge, the UN Commission and American imperialism, and covered the 8 February inauguration of the Korean People's Army. Kim Il-sung announced 1948 production quotas. The draft North Korean constitution (102 articles, ten chapters) was broadcast 16 February. The section also reports riots and an alleged 12 February border clash.

sections.title: Part VI: Social
sections.summary: Health, education, culture, press, youth and women.

sections.title: Section 1: Public Health and Welfare
sections.summary: A study found 62,198 of 173,305 deaths in April-December 1946 were children under five, about 40 per cent preventable with penicillin or sulfonamides. Typhus, typhoid and diphtheria were the main diseases; the National Venereal Disease Center and the 14 February prostitution ban were covered. Also reported: penicillin shipment, hospital conferences, nursing and veterinary courses, drug supplies, narcotics training, diphtheria toxoid and refugee camp welfare.

sections.title: Section 2: Education
sections.summary: February education report: provincial education directors met 18-19 February; middle school tuition rises from 600 to 1,800 won from 1 April, elementary tuition abolished; elementary budget cut to 1,600 million won subsidy. Teacher certification standards set, 500,000 surplus textbooks obtained, 182 English teachers finished American Language Institute course, and schooling figures since liberation tabulated.

sections.title: Section 3: Culture
sections.summary: Culture: essay explains the Tai Guk symbol on the Korean flag and its yin-yang philosophy; year 4281 celebrated 10 February. Museum director Kim Che-won and Kim Won-yong win Rockefeller fellowships. Monument to Admiral Li Sun-sin planned; Mozart concerts, opera, first New Korean Dictionary volume, HLKA's 21st anniversary, new HL amateur radio prefix, exhibits and a Chunchon library opened.

sections.title: Section 4: Press and Public Opinion
sections.summary: Press centered on the UN Temporary Commission, with calls for unity after Gandhi's murder. Papers covered the 7-10 February strikes (8,479 arrests by 26 February), clashed over police reform, and followed the prostitution-abolition law and the 7,000,000 won bribery scandal. Inflation and falling prices were debated; opinion polls and Department of Public Information outputs are reported.

sections.title: Section 5: Korean National Youth, Inc.
sections.summary: Study of Korean National Youth, Inc.: the 22-23 February council of 227 delegates re-elected Lee Bum-suk as president. Leftist infiltration during the 7 February riots was blocked and membership re-screened; membership reached 519,938 against a 600,000 goal. Reports cover training schools (curriculum of 209 hours), community service, new women's and student committees, and opposition.

sections.title: Section 6: Women's Activities
sections.summary: Women's activities: Korean women served as hostesses for the UN Commission, breaking custom, and hold posts in legislature, police, nursing and universities. Women's Bureau (founded September 1946, Director Koh Whang-kyung) published "New Homemaking" and moved to Hokuksa Temple on 27 February. Altrusa Club heard Mrs. Nixon and awarded a nursing fellowship; YWCA began English, night school and dressmaking classes.

sections.title: Back matter
sections.summary: Pages 494-499 hold no report content: blank Google-digitized pages, a back-cover image, a library date-due slip (stamped June 2010) and a final page of repeated meaningless OCR math symbols.
